digest.definition: The study of what it is to be human, past and present, from the microscopic to the global, drawing on many disciplines and on students' own lived experience
distinctiveFeatures: The study of what it is to be human, past and present, from the microscopic to the global, drawing on many disciplines and on students' own lived experience
Its outlook is global and comparative, avoids ranking cultural practices and holds that knowledge is situated, so many perspectives must be heard
Two main branches, Social and Biological Anthropology, with Anthropology in practice and Ethics as organising themes; courses may be general or focus on one sub-field
Intensely practical: it is learned by doing, through fieldwork, laboratory work and research projects from the start of study
Ethics and reflexivity are central: privilege in studying humans and primates, power imbalances with communities and students' own biases
Self-critical about its colonial origins and committed to decolonial work and to voices beyond the global North
It studies dynamic relationships among people, primates, hominins, things, bodies, environments and infrastructures

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Anthropology degree

statements.appliesTo: Anthropology degrees
statements.about: flexible, accessible routes for diverse students
statements.paraphrase: Degrees in the subject should be flexible and accessible and open routes to students from non-traditional backgrounds and with a range of disabilities and neurodivergent conditions; institutional support works alongside, helped by the varied nature of the discipline.

forPractitioner.text: Design the degree to be flexible and accessible, with routes in and through it for students from non-traditional backgrounds and for disabled and neurodivergent students; link this with the institution's own support services.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and the institution; the student meets its effect, not a standard to reach

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Anthropology degree

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject
statements.about: research projects from the start and the skills they build
statements.paraphrase: Students of the subject are required to design, carry out and finish research projects from the start of their studies; this builds skills in handling evidence and uncertainty, ethics, collaboration, detail, negotiation and networking, as well as a range of communication and transferable skills.

forPractitioner.text: Build research projects into the course from the first year: students are required to design, run and complete them, and through them develop skills in evidence, uncertainty, ethics, collaboration and communication across media.

forBeneficiary.text: From the start of your studies you must plan, carry out and finish your own research projects; through them you build skills in working with evidence, handling uncertainty, spotting ethical problems, working with others and communicating in many forms.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Anthropology degree

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject
statements.about: learning the subject by doing it
statements.paraphrase: The discipline is strongly practical: students are required to practise it, not only study it, building skills in a range of methods for collecting and analysing data that help them grasp how others, including the long dead, live their lives.

forPractitioner.text: Teach the subject as practice: students are required to do anthropology and not only learn about it, so plan for them to build skills in a range of methods for collecting and analysing data.

forBeneficiary.text: You must do anthropology, not only read about it: you build skills in several ways of collecting and analysing data so you can understand how other people, even those long dead, experience life.

headingPath: Context and purposes of an Anthropology degree

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject
statements.about: reflexive methods: confronting one's own biases
statements.paraphrase: Practical skills come through core methods courses suited to the degree's focus, which bring in ethics and collaboration with participants and co-researchers; the methods require students to confront their own biases and assumptions, see how academic research is placed in history and culture and grasp how this shapes readings of present and past.

forPractitioner.text: Make methods courses a core part of the programme, matched to its sub-disciplinary focus, with ethics and collaborative work built in; the methods require students to examine their own biases, see research as placed in history and culture and understand how that shapes interpretation.

forBeneficiary.text: Your methods training requires you to question your own biases and assumptions, see that research always comes from a particular time and culture, and understand how that shapes what we make of the present and the past.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Anthropology degree

statements.appliesTo: Anthropology degrees
statements.about: chances to weigh the ethics of research practices
statements.paraphrase: Anthropologists work to strict ethical guidelines; ethics is best woven through the degree, and students should be given chances to consider how different kinds of fieldwork suit different questions and settings, yield different findings and raise different ethical issues.

forPractitioner.text: Weave ethics through the degree, with dedicated modules where useful, and give students chances to consider how different fieldwork practices fit different questions and contexts, produce different outputs and carry different ethical demands.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course to give opportunities; its outcome for the student is 2.10

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Anthropology degree

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject by the end of the degree
statements.about: handling sensitive topics and complex ethics
statements.paraphrase: By the end of the degree students will have met and gained experience in handling sensitive topics, will understand complex ethical issues in context and will judge and build projects to the highest ethical standards.

forPractitioner.text: By graduation, students will have handled sensitive topics, will understand complex ethical issues in their context and will evaluate and develop projects against the highest ethical standards; plan exposure and practice to match.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you will have dealt with sensitive topics, you will understand complex ethical questions in their setting and you will be able to judge and shape projects to the highest ethical standards.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Anthropology degree

statements.appliesTo: joint honours, major-minor and combined studies students
statements.about: core skills on joint and combined degrees
statements.paraphrase: Students on joint, major-minor or combined degrees will reach the core subject-specific and generic skills of the subject and add others from their other subjects, and may explore where the subjects overlap.

forPractitioner.text: On joint, major-minor and combined routes, students will achieve the core subject-specific and generic skills and add others from the partner subjects; design for interdisciplinary overlap where it helps.

forBeneficiary.text: If you study the subject jointly or as part of a combined degree, you will gain its core subject and general skills and add others from your other subjects, with chances to explore where they meet.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Anthropology degree

statements.appliesTo: courses and students doing fieldwork
statements.about: communities as partners and co-producers
statements.paraphrase: Courses are likely to help students build partnerships and networks for employability and community work; fieldwork needs local communities, which should be treated as partners and, where fitting, as co-producers of knowledge, and working with them builds research design and wider employability skills.

forPractitioner.text: Plan partnerships with communities and organisations that suit the provider's specialisms; in fieldwork, local communities should be treated as partners and, where appropriate, as co-producers of knowledge, engaged in person or online as fits.

forBeneficiary.text: When your fieldwork involves a community, you should treat its members as partners and, where it fits, as people who create knowledge with you; working this way also builds your skills in research design, communication and planning.

headingPath: Distinctive features of an Anthropology degree

statements.appliesTo: Anthropology degrees
statements.about: introduction to professional organisations
statements.paraphrase: Students should be introduced, within their studies and career development, to the resources and networks of the professional organisations that fit their studies, chiefly the British Association for Biological Anthropology and Osteoarchaeology (BABAO) and the Royal Anthropological Institute (RAI).

forPractitioner.text: Introduce students, within the course and their career planning, to the resources and networks of the relevant professional organisations, chiefly BABAO and the RAI.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course; the student benefits from the introduction

statements.appliesTo: graduates of the subject
statements.about: knowing the range of methods and choosing them
statements.paraphrase: Degrees are likely to include substantial practical and empirical work; students need not graduate expert in every method, but they should know the range of methods available and be able to pick suitable ones for different research settings.

forPractitioner.text: Include practical, empirical data collection suited to the department's focus; graduates should know the range of methods and be able to choose suitable ones for a given research context, without being expert in all.

forBeneficiary.text: You will not need to master every method, but you should know the range of methods available and be able to choose the right ones for different kinds of research.

statements.appliesTo: all Anthropology degree courses
statements.about: the history of the discipline in every course
statements.paraphrase: Every degree in the subject will include the history of the discipline, Social and Biological alike, usually covering how theory and fieldwork developed, how its data have been read and used in the past and how it now takes active positions on current issues.

forPractitioner.text: Include the history of the discipline, both Social and Biological Anthropology, in every course: theoretical trends, fieldwork and practical techniques, past uses of data and the discipline's present engagement with social, economic and environmental questions.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a statement of what the course includes; its outcomes for the student are knowledge and understanding items 2, 11 and 18

statements.appliesTo: students of the subject
statements.about: colonialism, decolonising and a voice of one's own
statements.paraphrase: The discipline recognises its roots in European colonialism; students will learn why and how anthropologists try to decolonise the discipline and academia, meet critiques of academia's wider structures and be encouraged and trained to find their own voices in these debates.

forPractitioner.text: Teach how colonialism shaped the discipline and the lives it studied, and why and how decolonising work is done; students will be supported and trained to form positions of their own in these debates.

forBeneficiary.text: You will learn how colonialism shaped the subject and the communities it studied and why and how people work to decolonise the discipline and universities, and you will be helped to find your own voice in these debates.

statements.appliesTo: Anthropology degree courses
statements.about: ethical conduct, power and equitable collaboration
statements.paraphrase: Teaching on practice and method should include open debate about anthropologists' ethical conduct and their likely privilege and power over those they study; it should stress that interpretation is contested, that communities deserve respect, credit and the right to contest how they are shown, and that equitable collaboration is owed and rewarding; data sharing and open data should also be discussed where ethical and practicable.

forPractitioner.text: Pair methods teaching with explicit debate on ethical conduct and power imbalances; stress contested interpretation, respect and credit for communities as collaborators and their right to contest representation; and cover equitable sharing of data and outcomes, and open data, where ethical and practicable.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on teaching; the student meets its outcome in knowledge and understanding item 15 and subject-specific skills item 12

statements.appliesTo: Anthropology degree courses
statements.about: humans and their environments
statements.paraphrase: A further major focus will be the two-way relations between people and their environments, other species included; courses will usually encourage students to weigh the economic, ecological, ideological and cultural sides of those relations and what they mean for sustainability, conservation and the climate emergency.

forPractitioner.text: Make the relations between people and environments, other species included, a major focus, and encourage students to consider their economic, ecological, ideological and cultural aspects and what they mean for sustainability, conservation and climate.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a statement of course focus; the student meets its outcomes in knowledge and understanding items 8 and 14

statements.appliesTo: Anthropology degree courses
statements.about: familiarity with theoretical approaches
statements.paraphrase: Courses should make students familiar with the range of theoretical approaches to interpreting anthropological data, whether in a separate theory module or within problem-based study.

forPractitioner.text: See that students become familiar with the range of theoretical approaches for interpreting data, through a dedicated theory module or built into problem-oriented teaching.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course; the student meets its outcomes in knowledge and understanding item 10 and subject-specific skills item 5

statements.appliesTo: Anthropology degree courses
statements.about: work beyond the global North
statements.paraphrase: Because the discipline is global and needs many voices, courses should attend to work beyond the global North and look past contrasts between British, European and American traditions.

forPractitioner.text: Include developments in the discipline from beyond the global North, not only differences between UK, European and US traditions.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on curriculum design; the student meets it as content

statements.appliesTo: degrees focused on Social Anthropology
statements.about: everyday practices in Social Anthropology degrees
statements.paraphrase: Degrees focused on Social Anthropology will attend to the variety and social meaning of everyday practices, and courses should explore how social activities and institutions are enacted and understood locally in many places and cultures.

forPractitioner.text: In a degree focused on Social Anthropology, cover the variety and social meaning of everyday practices and explore how social activities and institutions are enacted and understood locally across settings, using topics such as those listed in 3.11.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a statement of course content; the student meets its outcomes in knowledge and understanding items 11 to 14

statements.appliesTo: Anthropology degree courses
statements.about: placements and practical research projects
statements.paraphrase: Beyond classes, students should be helped to take up placements and practical research projects, globally where possible, so that they engage with the wider discipline and with the local communities it works with.

forPractitioner.text: Make placements and practical research projects available, abroad too where appropriate and possible, so students engage with the disciplinary community and with local communities.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course to facilitate; the student chooses whether to take it up

statements.appliesTo: Anthropology degree courses
statements.about: self-directed study and outside opportunities
statements.paraphrase: Students should also be able to take part in varied self-directed study, online and through problem-based and group learning, and where fitting in volunteering, placements, work and exchanges; building independent study supports lifelong learning.

forPractitioner.text: Enable a range of self-directed study, including virtual learning environments, problem-based and group learning, e-learning and distance learning, and where appropriate volunteering, placements, workplace and exchange opportunities.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course to enable; the student meets its outcome in generic skills item 2

statements.appliesTo: each degree programme
statements.about: assessment and feedback strategy; criteria in advance
statements.paraphrase: Every programme will set out a clear strategy for assessment and feedback that lets students show and reflect on their attainment and development, and each assignment's aims, requirements and criteria will be set out and shared in advance.

forPractitioner.text: Set a clear assessment and feedback strategy for the programme, and for every assignment define its aims, requirements and generic and specific criteria and share them with students ahead of time.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the programme; the student benefits from clear criteria

statements.appliesTo: each degree programme
statements.about: assessment that avoids disadvantage
statements.paraphrase: Assessment is flexible to suit students' varied backgrounds and needs; the mix of formal methods should be designed so as not to disadvantage groups of students systematically, and adjustments are considered for individuals while outcomes are met fairly across the cohort.

forPractitioner.text: Design the combination of assessment methods so it does not systematically disadvantage any group of students, and consider adjustments for individuals while keeping outcomes fair and equitable across the cohort.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on assessment design; the student may ask about adjustments

statements.appliesTo: each degree programme
statements.about: varied assessment; marking group work
statements.paraphrase: Assessment in the subject has become very varied and is moving away from traditional essays and exams; work may be individual or in groups, and for group work the marking scheme will make clear how credit is shared among individuals.

forPractitioner.text: Use a wide range of assessment styles suited to each programme's outcomes; where work is done in groups, make sure the marking scheme states clearly how credit is split among individuals.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on assessment design; the student meets its effect in clear marking

statements.appliesTo: all Anthropology degrees
statements.about: reflective, critical analysis and use of evidence
statements.paraphrase: Whatever the form of assessment, every degree in the subject will stress reflective, critical analysis, the evaluation and fitting use of varied evidence and how it might help with real problems.

forPractitioner.text: Across all assessment, emphasise reflective and critical analysis, the evaluation and appropriate use of different kinds of evidence and its application to real-world problems.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a statement of what assessment emphasises; its outcomes for the student are subject-specific skills items 3 and 7 and generic skills item 5

statements.appliesTo: Anthropology degree courses
statements.about: dissertation and practical data collection
statements.paraphrase: Most students will complete a dissertation or extended research project, usually in the final year, showing skills across the research process; a practical data-collection, field or laboratory element should be encouraged and supported where suitable, though a project may rest on synthesis of secondary data.

forPractitioner.text: Offer a dissertation or extended research project, usually in the final year, covering the research process from framing questions to communicating findings; encourage and support a practical field, laboratory or data-collection element where appropriate, while allowing projects built on secondary data.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course to encourage and support; the dissertation is described for most students, not required of all

statements.appliesTo: each higher education provider
statements.about: using Annex D for achievement above threshold

statements.paraphrase: As the minimum for the honours degree, the graduate will have shown that they can engage with cultures, populations and groups unlike their own while keeping a personal judgement, aware of cultural assumptions, their own included, and show that they know how those assumptions affect the reading of others.

forPractitioner.text: Threshold: plan teaching and assessment so that every honours graduate on a degree mainly in Social Anthropology shows they can engage with cultures, populations and groups unlike their own while keeping a personal judgement, aware of cultural assumptions, their own included, and show that they know how those assumptions affect the reading of others.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your honours degree you will, as a minimum, be able to engage with cultures, populations and groups unlike your own while keeping a personal judgement, aware of cultural assumptions, your own included, and show that they know how those assumptions affect the reading of others.

statements.about: choosing techniques for research questions

statements.about: ethical issues and conduct in research
